new_statements.quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. [...] From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress. (p. 413) — Discussion of phonetics and phonology, in the remainder of this chapter, is based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages, for which the greatest information is available. (p. 407)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only modern description (Crowley & Dixon 1981, whose phonology rests mainly on this mid-eastern language and on South-eastern) can say only that stress never falls on the final syllable: disyllables are stressed initially, trisyllables on the first or the second syllable. The position is thus non-final but otherwise not predictable from the 19th-century transcriptions and the few recordings. The older and later sources disagree: Milligan 1859 (whose 'Oyster Bay to Pitwater' column is the largest Oyster Bay corpus) says only that the vowel before a double consonant or consonant cluster carries the accent; Ritz 1909 says the accent was 'quite frequently' antepenultimate and variable between speakers; Taylor 2006 argues from the recorders' bar diacritics for strong initial stress and rejects Crowley & Dixon's conclusion. No fixed-position reading is safely supported.
new_statements.exceptions: Crowley & Dixon: trisyllables vary between first- and second-syllable stress; Milligan's statement 'perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress' (weight-like conditioning, unverified); Ritz: accent placement 'at random or at will' between speakers; Taylor: 99% of diacritic-bearing initial word elements carry the stress bar.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms in wordlists recorded 1826-1859 by non-linguists; the Fanny Cochrane Smith wax cylinders and Crowley's 1972 five-word recording of Mrs Heffernan/Mrs Mundy are the only audio, and the authors say only stress placement can be inferred from the cylinders). Extinct language; no native-speaker phonetic data.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley & Dixon 1981 describe 'Tasmanian' as a whole but state (p. 407) that their phonology rests mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages; 'mid-eastern' = their language (a) Oyster Bay, Big River, Little Swanport = Glottolog oyst1235 (ISO xpd; AUSTLANG T2 Paredarerme / T3 Big River), so this is the variety the stress statement most directly covers, alongside South-eastern (brun1235 Bruny Island + sout1439). The same p. 413 statement is the statement of record for the sibling Tasmanian entries (tasm1247 bookkeeping node, brun1235, sout1439, sout3391, neta1235, benl1235); if the catalog wants one Tasmanian row, oyst1235 and brun1235 are the two varieties it actually rests on. Milligan 1859's accent note applies to his 'Tribes from Oyster Bay to Pitwater' column (Oyster Bay proper, collected at Wybalenna 1844-47, possibly a settlement lingua franca per Crowley & Dixon p. 397).
